answer: A market I find genuinely fascinating is the old bazaar in the centre of Sirajganj, which has been trading for as long as anyone can remember. I love wandering through it whenever I get the chance, usually on a weekend morning. It is a wonderfully [[vibrant]] place, with narrow lanes crammed with stalls selling everything from fresh vegetables, fish and spices to fabrics and handicrafts. Because our district is well known for handloom weaving, there are also shops piled high with colourful saris, lungis and gamchas, many of them made by weavers in nearby villages. The colours, smells and sounds combine to create an atmosphere that is completely [[immersive]]. What I enjoy most is the lively art of haggling, which is expected and almost a game between buyer and seller. I usually go there to buy fresh produce for my mother or small gifts, though half the fun is simply browsing. Before Eid I always buy a new lungi there for my grandfather, because he insists that local cloth is better than anything from Dhaka. The market has a raw, [[authentic]] character that modern shopping malls completely lack. Honestly, there is something special about a place where commerce has happened the same way for generations. Of course, it can be muddy and chaotic during the monsoon, but I have learnt to [[take that in my stride]]. It feels genuinely alive, and I always come away with a small treasure and a real sense of having experienced something [[quintessentially]] local.

followUps.q: Do you think traditional markets will survive?
followUps.answer: I hope so, and I think they will, at least in towns like mine. Many people still prefer fresh food and a personal relationship with sellers, although supermarkets and online shopping are slowly attracting younger customers.
Not as good as my mother, who is an expert. I usually start too high and give in too quickly, so when I need something important, I take her with me.

note: 'Old part of my city' changed to the old bazaar in Sirajganj; added the district's handloom tradition, shopping for his mother and grandfather; added mark 'take that in my stride'.
